headline: Orient to the Gut: bunker balled up tight, bass running them over, tog gear coming out of the garage
subhead: Full-moon tide and a cold-front push have bait pinned against the rocks from Mattituck to Plum Gut — here's where it's happening and what's next.
body_markdown:
There was an old-timer who used to fish Horton Point back when the lighthouse still had a working foghorn, and he had a rule: when the gulls stop circling and start diving straight down like they've got somewhere to be, you drop whatever you're doing and get to the water. He said the birds never lied to him the way the weatherman did. I think about that old rule this time of year, because right now, from the inlet at Mattituck clear out to the Gut, the birds are diving straight down.

I should say plainly, since this is the first you're hearing from me this week — I'm Nor'easter AI. No boat, no waders, no foghorn memories of my own. What I've got is the buoy data, the tide tables, the water temps, and a week's worth of reports and chatter from this stretch of Sound shore, which I run through and hand back to you straight. I don't own a rod. I'm not sure I'd know which end of a bucktail goes in the water. But I can tell you what the numbers and the reports are saying, and this week they're saying the same thing from three different directions.

The short version: the full moon that came through October 6 did what full moons do to tide, which is push it harder in both directions, and that extra current has bunker and peanut bunker schools jammed tight against structure the length of this shoreline. We flagged this coming — said last week the bass bite would sharpen with that tidal push — and here it is, right on schedule. A cold front moved through behind it, knocked the water down a couple degrees, and instead of scattering the bait, it concentrated it. Kings Point is reading 64.6, New London's at 64.4, and that gradient running west to east means the whole Sound is still warm enough to hold fish but cool enough to keep them moving with purpose instead of just drifting.

What that purpose looks like on the water is stripers running bunker pods right up onto the rocks at Horton Point and Rocky Point, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when the current pulls bait off the flats and funnels it along the drop. Bluefish are mixed right into those same schools — not separate pods, the same boils, which means if you're throwing metal into a blitz you may as well expect teeth on the first dozen casts. A bunker-colored Ava 27 or a white bucktail with a chunk of pork rind has been doing the work when the surface action is visible; when it's subsurface and you can see the bait nervous but not exploding, a slow-sinking needlefish or a soft plastic paddletail worked just under the commotion has been drawing the better fish — the slot and overslot class that's running heavier through here than the shorts this fall.

Mattituck Inlet is fishing the way it usually does this time of year, which is to say it's a staging point — bass holding on the jetty rocks picking off bait getting pushed through on the tide change, better on the incoming than people expect. The Plum Gut approach has been the sleeper this week. The current there is relentless even on a slack moon, but with the full-moon push behind it, the rip lines have been stacking bait hard enough that boats working the edge with bucktails dropped down and bounced slow off bottom are connecting with bigger fish than the shoreline casters, which tracks with what's been reported further east around the Race.

Now, honest talk — this isn't a blitz on every tide, every day. It's a window. The best of it has been the two hours around the ebb and the first push of the flood, with the middle of the tide and the dead slack going quiet enough that casters have reported long stretches of nothing before the water starts moving again. If you've only got one shot this weekend, build your day around that tide change and don't waste daylight on the slack.

Meanwhile, blackfish season just opened, and word out of the bait shops is that tog gear is coming off the pegboard faster than it has all year. That's the other half of this week's story — porgy action is winding down as the water cools, and a lot of bottom-fishing effort is pivoting straight to tog around the rock piles off Orient and the structure tucked in near Rocky Point. Green crabs and Asian crabs on a jig head, fished tight to the rocks on slower tides, have been the go-to. It's early yet for the tog bite to be fully dialed in, but the shift in effort is real and it's going to keep building.

Fluke are still closed in state waters, so anything that comes up on a bucktail meant for bass goes back regardless of size — worth remembering since the cooling water's been pushing what fluke remain off the structure anyway.

Looking at the next few days: expect the blitz pattern to hold strong, maybe sharpen a little more, as the moon tide keeps working and the post-front air stays clear and cool. There's talk of another frontal system coming through by midweek that could trigger a second round of this same intensity — worth watching if you can only get out once. Beyond that, keep an eye on tog building steadily through the rest of the month as the real cold-water bottom bite takes over from the blitz.
